channel.title: Muhammad Ilham Rilambang: Writing
channel.description: Notes on the craft of iOS.

item.title: An audit week on a shipping exam app: fix by consequence, then fix your fixes
item.description: I ranked an audit backlog by what a failure costs a student, not by how long it takes. Then some fixes broke things of their own: a debugging library still in the binary, a coverage gate that could not fail, tests that slept. What I changed, in the order I would do it again.

item.title: What a year of AI-native iOS development still can't prove
item.description: I audited the agent setup behind a year of iOS work and scored it seven out of ten. Nine failure modes, each with the number that makes it concrete, and the two gaps that keep it from a ten.

item.title: Exam mode, one screen earlier
item.description: The lock used to start inside the paper, after the questions were visible. Moving it into preparation closed that gap, and the blocked screen turned out to be a copy problem before it was a layout problem.

item.title: MVVM to VIPER, part three: a rename and a confession
item.description: Third of three. VIPER fixed nothing Clean had not, except the last unowned thing, the screen. Six use cases, a router with one owner, forty-three packages down to nineteen, and the operations that made the migration survivable.

item.title: MVVM to VIPER, part two: the wall, and the bill for it
item.description: Second of three. Three targets per feature make the dependency graph a compiler fact, and forty-three packages make it a second product. The clean architecture win, and the cost I had not priced in.

item.title: MVVM to VIPER, part one: when the view model is the app
item.description: First of three. What MVVM gets right, what the proctored exam screen's view model quietly took ownership of, and why a pattern that works at five screens stops being local at fifty.

item.title: Four gates that passed without testing anything
item.description: A lint gate that linted a directory, a pre-push script that ran two thirds of the tests and printed success, a build number shared by three uploads, and snapshots that recorded a session instead of a screen. Every one was green, and every green was true about the wrong thing.

item.title: What a green build does not prove
item.description: Five things I described as verified this week that were not: a pipeline that compiled a working copy, a lock file that pinned a branch, a push I said would deploy once, a release that changed nothing, and an analytics field I called unused. Same mistake each time, a colour taken as evidence about inputs.

item.title: AI-native development is a process, not a feature
item.description: What I write down so an agent is useful inside a real codebase: the conventions file, the brief, the one piece of evidence I accept, and the parts I refuse to hand over.

item.title: The iOS stack I actually reach for
item.description: The stack I reach for on someone else's codebase, where every choice is priced by whether the next engineer can debug it at 3am.

item.title: How I review iOS pull requests
item.description: Risk before style, deletion before addition, and three questions I ask on every diff. What I refuse to merge, and why the comment that explains the failure mode is worth ten that state the rule.

item.title: A design system is a review policy, not a library
item.description: Importing a token package changes nothing. The system holds when the correct choice is easier than the wrong one, and when review refuses the local override.

item.title: UIKit to SwiftUI without a rewrite
item.description: The migration succeeds or fails on one decision: who owns navigation. Everything else is a sequence of small, reversible steps.

item.title: Build time is a dependency-graph problem, not a machine problem
item.description: Faster hardware buys you a constant factor. The graph is the exponent. Why the first fix is almost always deleting a script phase, and what to measure before you touch anything.

item.title: Splitting an app into local Swift packages: what breaks first
item.description: The files move in a day. The boundaries take a quarter. Here is the order things actually break in, and the one rule that keeps the first week from turning into a public-API explosion.

item.title: Kiosk and assessment apps: what Apple will and won't let you lock
item.description: You don't own the device, iOS does. What an exam app can actually lock, what Apple already enforces, and the entitlement to ask for in week one.
